summary: Defines EAP-EKE, an authentication method for the Extensible Authentication Protocol based on the Encrypted Key Exchange protocol. It gives mutual authentication using a short, easy-to-remember password. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A way to log in to a network with a short password where both sides prove they know it, without sending the password itself.

subtitle: Password-based authentication that resists dictionary attacks and requires no certificates.

tldr.problem: People choose passwords they can remember, which means passwords are weak by cryptographic standards. Without proper protection, an attacker with the ability to try password guesses can break in through dictionary attacks, testing every password in a dictionary until one works.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-EKE implements the Encrypted Key Exchange protocol as an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) method. Two parties exchange encrypted ephemeral Diffie-Hellman public keys, protected by the user's password, then verify each other's identity by proving knowledge of the password through cryptographic challenges, all without the password ever being transmitted.
tldr.outcome: Both parties achieve mutual authentication and derive strong, random session keys. An attacker can only guess one password per attempt, preventing dictionary attacks. No public-key certificates are required, making deployment simpler than certificate-based methods.

today: RFC 6124 defines EAP-EKE as an Informational RFC. The method has seen implementation and deployment in various EAP-capable networks, particularly in wireless and access control systems where passwords are the primary authentication mechanism and certificate management would be impractical.

sections.title: The Password Authentication Problem
sections.content:
Most Internet access requires a username and password. Users choose passwords they can remember and type easily, which limits entropy: a typical user password carries only 20 to 30 bits of security, far below the 128 bits or more that cryptographic algorithms require. An attacker with access to capture the messages exchanged during authentication can attempt a dictionary attack: try every password in a dictionary and see which one works, testing thousands of guesses in seconds on modern hardware.

EAP-EKE solves this problem through the Encrypted Key Exchange (EKE) protocol, originally proposed by Bellovin and Merritt in 1992. The protocol encrypts cryptographic values with the password itself, so an attacker cannot verify a password guess without interacting with the server. An active attacker can make only one password guess per protocol run, making dictionary attacks infeasible even against weak passwords. EAP-EKE implements this protocol as a method for the Extensible Authentication Protocol, allowing deployment over wireless networks, dial-in systems, and other EAP-capable networks.
sections.eli5: When logging in with a weak password, an attacker who sees the messages cannot just try every word in a dictionary. EAP-EKE makes them prove they know the password by doing a special math puzzle.

sections.title: The Three-Message Exchange
sections.content:
EAP-EKE authentication proceeds in three phases. First, the Identity exchange (EAP-EKE-ID) allows the server and peer to exchange their identities and negotiate cryptographic algorithms (the Diffie-Hellman group, encryption cipher, hash function, and message authentication code). The server sends proposals in priority order; the peer selects one.

Second, the Commit exchange (EAP-EKE-Commit) is where the key exchange happens. The server generates an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman private key x_s and computes its public key y_s = g^x_s (mod p). It encrypts this public key using a key derived from the password, creating DHComponent_S. The peer does the same, generating y_p and DHComponent_P. The peer also generates a random challenge (nonce) Nonce_P, encrypts and protects it using keys derived from the Diffie-Hellman shared secret, and sends it as PNonce_P. Both parties compute the shared secret: SharedSecret = g^(x_s * x_p) (mod p).

Third, the Confirm exchange (EAP-EKE-Confirm) proves liveness and knowledge of the password. The server sends Nonce_P combined with its own nonce Nonce_S, both encrypted and authenticated with keys derived from the shared secret, plus an authentication tag Auth_S that signs all previous messages. The peer replies with Nonce_S and its own authentication tag Auth_P. If both sides computed the same shared secret, their authentication tags match, proving mutual authentication.
sections.eli5: First, they agree on which encryption methods to use. Next, they swap secret numbers that are scrambled with the password so neither can prove to an eavesdropper that the password is right. Finally, they prove to each other they got the same secret number by doing a math puzzle.

sections.title: Why This Protects Weak Passwords
sections.content:
EAP-EKE protects weak passwords through a simple but powerful idea: the encrypted Diffie-Hellman public key (DHComponent) can only be decrypted and verified by someone who knows the correct password. An attacker capturing the protocol messages sees ciphertext that could be produced by any of billions of possible passwords; trying a dictionary attack means running the decryption and checking whether the decrypted value is a valid Diffie-Hellman public key. For each wrong password, the decrypted value will be random noise, not a valid key, so the attacker learns nothing.

The Commit exchange phase crucially commits both parties to their Diffie-Hellman values before either can produce a proof. This prevents an attacker from trying different public key values against captured ciphertexts. The authentication tags in the Confirm exchange ensure that modifying the negotiated algorithms would be detected immediately. Moreover, even if an attacker somehow obtained the shared secret, the password cannot be recovered from it, providing forward secrecy: compromise of session keys does not reveal the password.
sections.eli5: The scrambled number only looks right if you unscramble it with the correct password. An attacker cannot check if a guess is right without talking to the real server, so they cannot guess thousands of times at once.

sections.title: Algorithms and Key Derivation
sections.content:
EAP-EKE is a framework that negotiates which cryptographic algorithms to use. The negotiated parameters include the Diffie-Hellman group (the mathematical group in which the key exchange happens), the encryption cipher (such as AES-128 in CBC mode), the pseudo-random function (PRF) (such as HMAC-SHA1) for key derivation, and the message authentication code (MAC) (such as HMAC-SHA1 for authenticating messages).

Key material is derived using a two-step process inspired by HKDF (HMAC-based Key Derivation Function). First, the PRF is applied to zero octets and the password to produce a temporary key, then to that key and the participant identities to produce the encryption key for DHComponent. After both parties compute the shared secret, they perform an extraction step, applying the PRF to zero octets and the shared secret, then expanding to produce the encryption key (Ke) and integrity key (Ki) for all subsequent messages. This design ensures that even slight differences in password produce completely different keys, and every session with the same password generates different keys.
sections.eli5: They choose standard encryption and hash algorithms. They use the password and math puzzles to create separate scrambling keys for this session so no two sessions look the same.

sections.title: Resistance to Attacks and Security Properties
sections.content:
EAP-EKE satisfies the key security requirements for password-based authentication. It is resistant to passive attacks (eavesdropping): an attacker who sees the messages learns nothing useful about the password or the session key. It is resistant to active attacks (message modification, replay, or insertion): a modified ciphertext will fail decryption or integrity checks, and an attacker cannot replay old messages because nonces are verified. Most importantly, it resists dictionary attacks: an attacker gains no computational advantage; each wrong password guess requires a fresh protocol interaction, making large-scale offline attacks impossible.

The protocol provides mutual authentication: both the peer and server prove possession of the password through cryptographically binding authentication tags that include all previous messages. It provides forward secrecy: if the password is later compromised, session keys from earlier runs remain secret. The only unprotected element is the participant identities, which must be sent in plaintext for the server to locate the password. Implementations can address identity hiding through application-level mechanisms if needed. Overall, the design reflects careful cryptographic engineering that has withstood academic scrutiny since the original 1992 EKE proposal and subsequent security improvements.
sections.eli5: An eavesdropper learns nothing. Someone who tries to change the messages is caught. Trying to guess the password by doing the protocol costs the attacker real time talking to the server, not just computer time. If the password is discovered later, old sessions are still secret.
